title: For energy security, E100 alone is not the answer
where: The Editorial Page, page 12 (A Das, CSEP)
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Conservation; Government policies · GS2 › Energy security and foreign policy
summary: After E20 and a rules change that allows pure-ethanol (E100) vehicles, the writer argues ethanol cannot cut crude imports much unless biofuel policy also tackles diesel.
ideas: Policy has moved fast: India has made the transition to E20 petrol, and an amendment to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 now allows vehicles to run on pure ethanol (E100).
GS3 · Energy policy
The move from E20 to E100 shows biofuels becoming a pillar of India's energy-security strategy.
The barrel limits the gain: petrol is only 15-18% of what a barrel of crude yields, while diesel is about 44-45%, so ethanol addresses a small slice of oil demand.
GS3 · Energy security
Ethanol can only displace petrol, a minor share of the crude barrel, so its import savings are limited.
Diesel is the real dependence: India consumed about 503 million tonnes of diesel against 200 million tonnes of petrol (FY21-FY25); freight, farming and logistics run on it.
GS3 · Energy / Infrastructure
Diesel, not petrol, drives India's oil demand, so biofuel policy must target diesel.
Less petrol does not mean less crude: refineries can shift product yields only a little, so petrol displaced is not the same as crude imports reduced.
GS3 · Energy security
Policymakers must separate petrol displaced, spending avoided and actual reduction in crude imports.
Measure outcomes, not volumes: biodiesel lags its 5% target; success should be judged by lower crude demand and import bills, not litres of ethanol blended.
GS3 · Policy evaluation
The test of biofuel policy is reduced import dependence, not the volume of ethanol blended.
keywords: Limited flexibility to change the mix of products from a barrel
Refinery yield rigidity means cutting petrol demand does not cut crude throughput proportionately.
Measuring litres blended versus imports avoided
Biofuel policy should track outcomes such as imports avoided, not outputs like blending rates.
Vulnerability to price and supply shocks from imported oil
With over 80% of crude imported, India's import exposure makes West Asian conflicts a domestic risk.
Ethanol carries less energy than petrol, cutting fuel economy
Ethanol's lower energy content means a 20% blend cuts petrol use by less than 20%.
Reliable supply of raw material for biofuels
Scaling biodiesel needs feedstock security from non-edible oils and used cooking oil.
data: Share of India's crude oil requirement that is imported
India imports over 80% of its crude oil, leaving it exposed to price and geopolitical shocks.
Share of each in products from a barrel of crude
Petrol is only 15-18% of the crude barrel; diesel is 44-45%.
Diesel vs petrol consumed, FY 2020-21 to FY 2024-25
India used about 503 million tonnes of diesel and 200 million tonnes of petrol in FY21-FY25.
Modelled fall in petrol consumption from a 20% ethanol blend
E20 may cut petrol use by about 15.56%, not 20%, because ethanol has lower energy content.
examples: E20 rollout
India's transition to 20% ethanol-blended petrol
GS3 · Energy / Agriculture
The E20 rollout shows how biofuels can link farm income with energy security.
West Asia conflict and oil trade
The ongoing conflict has disrupted oil trade, the writer notes
GS2 · Energy security and foreign policy
The West Asia conflict shows why diversifying away from imported oil is a strategic need.
Used cooking oil for biodiesel
Past efforts on non-edible oils and used cooking oil faced feedstock and supply-chain hurdles
GS4
GS3 · Waste to energy / GS4 · Environmental ethics
Turning used cooking oil into biodiesel joins waste management with energy security.
pyqs: Challenges to energy security and measures: the petrol-diesel asymmetry is a sharp point.
Energy security and foreign policy in West Asia: import exposure is the link.
India's energy cooperation with West Asia: biofuels reduce but do not end dependence.
Refinery location and its implications: refinery economics shape import needs.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from cooperation with West Asia (2017) to energy security as the core of foreign policy (2025) and, in 2026, to the challenges of energy security alongside growth and sustainability. Geography touched refineries (2017).
trend.watch: Energy security has been asked in 2017, 2025 and 2026, in both GS2 and GS3. Prepare it as a cross-paper topic: diplomacy, domestic supply and transition.
focus: Import dependence and diversification of suppliers
Biofuels, EVs and the energy transition
West Asia, sea lanes and energy diplomacy

potential: "Ethanol blending can reduce petrol consumption, but not India's dependence on imported crude in the same proportion." Examine. (15 marks)

parts: Introduction: E20 to E100, with facts

answer.t: India has moved to E20 and amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 to allow E100, while it still imports over 80% of its crude oil.

pts.t: A 20% blend can cut petrol use by about 15.56%.
Lower petrol demand reduces spending on its supply.
Sugarcane and grain feedstock link energy with rural incomes.
Distilleries and flex-fuel vehicles build an industry.
A domestic fuel softens the impact of crises.
pts.ex: The West Asia conflict has disrupted oil trade.

pts.t: It is only 15-18% of a crude barrel; diesel is 44-45%.
About 503 MT of diesel against 200 MT of petrol in FY21-FY25.
Refineries cannot freely raise diesel yields, so crude throughput falls little.
Ethanol's lower energy content reduces fuel economy.
The 5% target was missed; feedstock and supply chains are weak.
Counting litres blended overstates import savings.
R&D and blending targets for biodiesel and renewable diesel.
Collection of used cooking oil and non-edible oilseeds.
Track crude demand and import bills.
Electric trucks, rail freight and solar pumps cut diesel.
Reserves and diverse sources against shocks.

answer.t: The real test of India's biofuel strategy is how far it cuts imported oil, which means looking beyond the petrol pump to diesel.

title: Assam, north Bengal districts on high alert; 12,000 evacuated from areas along Sankosh
where: Nation, page 11 (Sweety Kumari & Shinjini Ghosh); Odisha cyclone report (Sujit Bisoyi), same page
syllabus: GS1 › Important geophysical phenomena; Changes in glaciers · GS3 › Disaster and disaster management · GS2 › India and its neighbourhood (Bhutan)
summary: A glacial lake outburst in Bhutan's Gasa region put Assam and north Bengal on alert along the Sankosh, while cyclone Arnab's rains caused landslides and floods in Odisha.
ideas: Hazards cross borders: a glacial lake burst in Bhutan's Gasa region, sending water, mud and debris downstream into Indian river systems along the Sankosh.
GS1 · Geophysical phenomena / GS2 · Neighbourhood
Glacial lake outbursts in the Himalaya are transboundary hazards needing shared early warning.
Early action saved lives: about 12,000 people along the Sankosh in Alipurduar were moved to safety, with public announcements and disaster forces on standby; no major damage was reported.
GS3 · Disaster preparedness
Timely evacuation turns a hazard into a non-disaster.
Cyclone impacts reach far inland: under cyclone Arnab, torrential rain set off landslides in Odisha's Kandhamal and Ganjam, killing a family, and left about 300 villages marooned in Ganjam.
GS3 · Disaster management / GS1 · Cyclones
Cyclone risk is not only coastal: inland landslides and floods follow the rain.
Recovery needs administrators: Odisha deputed more than 30 senior OAS officers to Ganjam for relief and restoration of roads, power and health services.
GS3 · Disaster response / GS2 · Governance
Disaster recovery depends on surge administrative capacity on the ground.
Warming raises the risk: as Himalayan glaciers melt, glacial lakes grow, so monitoring them is now part of climate adaptation.
GS1 · Glaciers / GS3 · Climate
Shrinking glaciers and growing lakes make GLOF monitoring a climate-adaptation priority.
keywords: Sudden release of water from a glacier-fed lake
GLOFs are rising with Himalayan glacier melt and can strike far downstream.
Sharing hazard data across national borders
The Sankosh alert shows the need for transboundary early warning with Bhutan.
One hazard triggering others (cyclone → rain → landslide → flood)
Cyclone Arnab's landslides show how disasters cascade.
Extra staff and resources deployed in a crisis
Deploying senior officers to Ganjam is surge capacity in action.
examples: Sankosh evacuation
About 12,000 people moved after a GLOF in Bhutan; no major disaster
GS3 · Disaster preparedness / GS2 · India–Bhutan
The Sankosh evacuation shows how early warning and quick action prevent a transboundary flood disaster.
Cyclone Arnab, Odisha
Landslides in Kandhamal; 300 villages marooned in Ganjam
GS4
GS3 · Disaster management / GS4 · Compassion in public service
Cyclone Arnab's inland landslides show that cyclone preparedness must extend to the hills.
pyqs: Melting Himalayan glaciers and India's water resources.
Shrinking Himalayan glaciers and climate change.
Disaster resilience and the Sendai Framework.
Infrastructure development vs disaster-risk reduction in ecologically sensitive areas.
potential: Glacial lake outburst floods are an emerging transboundary hazard in the Himalaya. Discuss the measures India should take, including cooperation with neighbours. (15 marks)

title: To ease energy transition, ramp up storage, strengthen transmission
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Investment models; Conservation
context: A former CEA member writes that India has moved from chronic power deficits to a solar-hour glut and night-time deficits. The answer, he argues, is storage, stronger transmission, demand-side management and markets that reward flexibility.
ideas: Capacity is not the goal; power when people need it, by night as well as by day, is.
GS3 · Energy transition
India has moved from shortages to a solar-hour surplus, but night-time deficits show capacity is not enough.
Storage is the bottleneck: pumped storage is slow to build and bid prices are said to be unremunerative.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Storage is the bottleneck of India's energy transition; pumped storage is slow to build.
Wasted solar power and constant ramping of coal plants are a double loss.
GS3 · Resource efficiency
Curtailed solar and constant ramping of coal plants are a double loss for the grid.
keywords: Midday solar glut, evening demand peak
India's grid now faces a duck curve: a midday solar glut and an evening demand peak.
Clean power supplied at all hours
Storage and transmission are needed to deliver round-the-clock clean power.
Forcing generators to cut output the grid cannot absorb
Without storage, solar power is curtailed, wasting cheap clean energy.
Shifting or cutting demand to balance the grid
Demand-side management can shift use to solar hours and ease the evening peak.
data: Renewable capacity incl. large hydro, and its share of the total
Renewables, including large hydro, are about 292 GW, roughly 53% of India's installed capacity.
India's solar capacity has reached about 162 GW.
Thirty years ago 40% of Indians had no electricity (World Bank); today India has a daytime surplus.
pyqs: Capacity is not the only target: a solar-hour glut with night deficits shows storage and transmission are the bottleneck.
Grid flexibility and storage as part of energy security.
Cheap solar now forces coal plants to ramp up and down, shortening their life.
where: The Editorial Page, page 12 (Somit Dasgupta (teaser on page 1))
summary: India now has surplus power in solar hours and shortages at night; a former CEA member argues storage and transmission are the missing pieces.
evolution: 30 years ago
40% of Indians had no electricity (World Bank, cited in the article).
Electricity Act allowed state electricity boards to be split into separate companies.
Around 2008
Power exchanges in Delhi and Mumbai led to a capacity boom; over 1,00,000 MW of coal capacity added 2010-2020.
About 292 GW renewables (53% of capacity), 162 GW solar; daytime glut, night deficit.

title: Govt notifies E100 as auto fuel for flex-fuel vehicles
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Environment (pollution); Agriculture-linked industry
context: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways amended the Central Motor Vehicle Rules to allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on up to E100 (nearly pure ethanol). Ordinary petrol or E20 vehicles cannot use E100.
ideas: Ethanol reduces dependence on imported crude oil.
GS3 · Energy security
Higher ethanol blends such as E100 cut India's dependence on imported crude.
Lower lifecycle emissions are possible, but they depend on the crop and the production process.
GS3 · Environment (balanced view)
Ethanol's climate benefit depends on the crop and process used, so lifecycle emissions must be counted.
keywords: Crops for ethanol compete with crops for food and water
Biofuel policy must manage the food-vs-fuel trade-off over land and water.
Vehicle built to run on different petrol-ethanol blends
Flex-fuel vehicles, now allowed to run on E100, offer a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
Emissions across production, transport and use
Judged by lifecycle emissions, not tailpipe alone, biofuels are not automatically green.
Ethanol blending reduces import dependence and the oil import bill.
pyqs: Higher ethanol blends reduce dependence on imported crude.
Flex-fuel vehicles as a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
links: Related Explained: Centre clears way for flex-fuel up to E100
summary: Flex-fuel vehicles may now run on E100, nearly pure ethanol; ordinary petrol and E20 vehicles cannot.
evolution: Before Oct 2026
Ongoing debate over the use of E20 fuel (as the report notes).
E100 notified, but only for vehicles built as flex-fuel.

title: Climate justice needs quicker compensation: first Loss and Damage payout to Nepal
syllabus: GS3 › Environment; Disaster management · GS2 › International institutions; India's neighbourhood · GS4 › Ethical issues in international funding
context: The UN's Fund for Loss and Damage has allocated $21.6 million (about Rs 190 crore) to Nepal, nearly two months after devastating floods. It is the first time the Fund has earmarked a grant for a disaster-affected nation. The Indian Express argues the episode should become a case study for reforming the Fund.
ideas: Loss and damage is compensation, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for climate change.
GS3 climate · GS2 global governance
Loss and damage finance is compensation owed, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for emissions.
Speed is justice: delays raise hardship and rebuilding costs, especially for poor countries.
GS3 DM · GS4 fairness
Delayed climate compensation is justice denied: it raises hardship and rebuilding costs.
Money is short: $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
GS3 · Climate finance
The Loss and Damage Fund has only $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
keywords: Climate harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent
Loss and damage covers harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent.
Sharing climate burdens by responsibility and capacity
Climate justice demands that burdens be shared by responsibility and capacity.
Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities
India's climate diplomacy rests on CBDR-RC: common but differentiated responsibilities.
Those who cause harm bear its cost
The polluter pays principle makes loss and damage a duty of high emitters.
data: Nepal emits barely 0.1% of global emissions yet suffers some of the worst climate disasters.
Pledged to the Fund, about a third of pending claims
Pledges of $822 million cover only about a third of pending loss-and-damage claims.
examples: Nepal: low emitter, high impact
Barely 0.1% of emissions, yet among the hardest hit
GS4
GS4 · Fairness
Nepal, a low emitter facing high losses, shows why climate justice is a moral question.
Avalanche-triggered floods in Nepal
An ice-and-rock avalanche set off flash floods and wrecked hydropower plants
Disaster answers
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods show cascading Himalayan hazards that destroy infrastructure.
pyqs: Loss-and-damage finance as part of climate commitments: first grant, $822 million pledged against far larger claims.
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods as a Himalayan climate hazard with cross-border lessons.
Nepal lost at least 10% of its hydropower facilities: infrastructure in fragile terrain.
Nepal's case shows who pays for 'development' driven by greed: low emitters, high losses.
links: Related Explained (Telegram): Why Rs 190 crore payout to Nepal matters
summary: The UN Fund for Loss and Damage made its first grant, to flood-hit Nepal; the Indian Express says payouts must be faster and the Fund reformed.
evolution: Fund for Loss and Damage created at COP27, after a nearly three-decade campaign by vulnerable nations.
Fund operationalised.
First grant earmarked, to Nepal; developed countries insisted it is an exception, not a precedent.
COP31 begins in Antalya, Turkey, with compensation on the agenda.

title: Punjab farm fires: why most stubble-burning incidents are in two districts
syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution; Cropping patterns; Agricultural technology · GS4 › Ethical dilemmas: private gain vs public good
context: Punjab has recorded 684 farm fires this season, 457 of them (69%) in Tarn Taran and Amritsar. Early harvesting of short-duration paddy in the Majha region lets farmers fit in a third crop of peas or potatoes before wheat, which leaves little time to clear fields without burning.
ideas: The real cause is the crop calendar, not just a lack of machines.
GS3 · Stubble burning
Stubble burning in Majha is driven by the crop calendar, not merely a lack of machines.
Fires are falling year on year; support and awareness matter as much as penalties.
GS3 policy · GS4 persuasion
Falling farm fires show that support and awareness work alongside penalties.
Leaving the paddy-wheat cycle is the long-term fix (see Manauli's sweet-corn shift).
GS3 · Crop diversification
Moving out of the paddy-wheat cycle, as Manauli did, is the long-term fix for stubble burning.
keywords: Farmers stuck in one crop cycle by MSP and habit
A paddy-wheat lock-in leaves farmers little choice but to burn straw before the next crop.
A private act that imposes costs on others
Stubble burning is a negative externality: a private saving that imposes health costs on millions.
Handling straw in the field / removing it for use elsewhere
In-situ and ex-situ residue management offer alternatives to burning.
Moving to a wider mix of crops
Crop diversification is the durable answer to stubble burning and groundwater stress.
data: Farm fires by this point in the season, 2024 → 2025 → 2026
Punjab's farm fires fell from 1,857 (2024) to 743 (2025) to 684 (2026) by the same point in the season.
Despite 1.25 lakh residue-management machines, Punjab still sees farm fires.
examples: Manauli, Haryana's 'sweet corn village'
About 70% of 2,000 acres moved from paddy to sweet corn and vegetables; farmers formed an FPO
Success story
Manauli in Haryana moved about 70% of its land from paddy to sweet corn and vegetables and formed an FPO.
pyqs: Majha's third crop and Manauli's shift to sweet corn show diversification in practice.
Why farmers choose high-value crops: Manauli's returns and market links.
Farm fires and clean air: 684 fires so far against 743 last year and 1,857 in 2024.
summary: Most of Punjab's farm fires this season are in Tarn Taran and Amritsar, where a third crop leaves farmers too little time to clear fields without burning.
evolution: 1,857 fires by this point in the season.
743 fires in the same period.
684 fires so far, but an early spike in Majha.

title: 'Godzilla' El Niño effects to be felt into 2027: decoding the WMO warning
syllabus: GS1 › Important geophysical phenomena; Climatology · GS3 › Food security; Disaster management
context: The World Meteorological Organization has warned that the intense 2026 El Niño will peak around year-end and affect weather well into 2027. It has already weakened India's southwest monsoon.
ideas: El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, causing drought and heatwaves.
GS1 climatology · GS3 drought
El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, bringing drought and heatwaves.
Effects into 2027 threaten food and water security and could push up fertiliser and fuel prices.
GS3 · Food security
The 2026 El Niño, lasting into 2027, threatens food and water security and could raise fertiliser and fuel prices.
keywords: Preparing farming and water systems to withstand dry years
Drought-proofing farming and water systems is the answer to recurring El Niño years.
Rising food prices after a poor harvest
A weak monsoon feeds food inflation, hurting the poor most.
Farming that relies on rain, not irrigation
Monsoon-dependent agriculture leaves India exposed to every El Niño.
One shock triggering others: drought, prices, water
El Niño brings cascading risks: drought, prices, water shortage.
data: Share of India's annual rain from the southwest monsoon
The southwest monsoon brings about 70% of India's annual rainfall.
India's 2026 monsoon, the fourth driest since 2001
India's 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of the long period average, the fourth driest since 2001.
pyqs: El Niño as a drought driver: the 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of LPA.
WMO warning: an El Niño strong enough to weaken the monsoon and affect weather into 2027.
Effects into 2027 on food and water security.
summary: The WMO warns that this year's intense El Niño, which already weakened India's monsoon, will affect weather well into 2027.
evolution: El Niño peaked at 2.3°C (NOAA data, cited in the report).
June 2026
Current El Niño emerged and intensified rapidly.
2026 monsoon
Ended at 87% of LPA, the fourth driest since 2001.
Into 2027
WMO expects effects to continue.
